title: Start with the Reported Problem
definition: A complaint or concern about treatment, conditions or a demand.
content:
A grievance is a complaint or concern. A cause is a factor that helps explain why something happened. A source may report a grievance without revealing every participants motive. To investigate resistance, ask what demand or treatment was challenged, who was involved and what evidence connects the concern with a recorded action.

The NHCP marker connects Sumuroys uprising in Palapag, Samar, beginning on 1 June 1649, with forced labor and abuses. This is a named connection between a concern and opposition, not a complete account of every participants thoughts. Our fictional report card separates a demand, a reported problem and an action. It is not an original testimony or an invented speech. Keep the place and period visible. Finding one grievance does not mean that every uprising elsewhere had the same cause or that the concern affected every household identically.

clues: Reported problem
A grievance concerns treatment, conditions or a demand.

The NHCP marker connects the Palapag uprising of 1649 with forced labor and abuses.
Scope
A stated grievance does not reveal every participants motive or every revolts cause.
task: A marker names forced labor and abuses in the Palapag case. What does that support?
A named grievance-action connection, not every participants full motive
Every revolt everywhere had one cause
Every household thought identically
The marker is a transcript of every conversation
reason: A named grievance-action connection, not every participants full motive. A stated grievance does not reveal every participants motive or every revolts cause.

title: A Policy Could Affect Work and Choices
definition: Exclusive control over a particular trade or activity.
content:
A policy could affect work, income and choices. To explain a protest, connect the rule with evidence of how it affected people. Do not replace that investigation with a claim that everyone automatically reacted the same way. A policy, a reported grievance and an uprising are related but different parts of the explanation.

The CCP account of the Basi Revolt connects the Ilocos uprising of 1807 with government monopoly over basi, a sugarcane wine. Here the historical question concerns regulation and control of production and sale. It is not an invitation to drink, make or handle alcohol. Our cause-and-action card does not reproduce graphic paintings or reconstruct every event of the revolt. The later painting series has its own making date and viewpoint. Use the source for the bounded policy connection, then seek further evidence for particular participants, motives and outcomes.

title: A Request Was Not the Same as an Uprising
definition: A formal request made to an authority.
content:
People could express opposition or seek changed terms in different ways. A petition asks an authority for something. An uprising involves collective opposition that can include armed conflict. These are different actions. A request for relief is not automatically a demand to end all colonial rule, and a complaint is not proof that fighting occurred.

The UP Diliman summary describes a 1698 Bacolor petition about tribute-collection duties. Compare that recorded request with the named uprising examples. This comparison does not turn every petition into a revolt or make petitions harmless in every possible setting. Ask what was requested and what action the source records. Our fictional sorting cards identify request, reported complaint and collective uprising without asking students to act out violence. Filing a petition also does not establish that every request was granted; its outcome needs separate evidence.

clues: Action type
A formal request and a collective uprising are different recorded actions.

reason: A request for changed terms was made; wider aims and results need evidence. Seeking changed terms does not automatically mean every demand was granted or all rule was rejected.

title: Participants Could Have Different Concerns
definition: Taking part in an activity or action.
content:
An uprising or petition could involve people with different roles, concerns and degrees of choice. A named leader is not every participants complete story. A place name also does not mean that every resident joined. To explain participation, ask which people are actually recorded and what the source says about their actions.

Our fictional source desk contains a leader summary, a list of participants and an account of affected households. They can answer different questions. Being affected is not necessarily the same as taking part. A list can establish a recorded name without explaining everything that person wanted. Do not assign a motive from a persons religion, ancestry or occupation. The model is not an authentic participant register for Sumuroy, Bacolor or Basi. Students do not disclose family identity or choose targets; the task is to interpret the evidence and its limits.

clues: Roles
Leaders, participants and affected residents need not be the same people.
Recorded action

No automatic motive

title: Keep Causes, Actions and Outcomes Separate
definition: What followed an action or process, as supported by evidence.
content:
A historical explanation connects causes, actions and outcomes without treating them as identical. A grievance can help explain an action; an aim describes what people sought; an outcome concerns what followed. Failure to achieve one aim does not make the grievance unreal, and recording a grievance does not prove that the action succeeded.

Use a fictional evidence chain: a reported demand, an account of opposition and a later record. Ask what each link supports. If the later record is missing, state uncertainty rather than invent success or failure. A later commemorative marker and a painting can preserve important interpretations, but they are not automatically eyewitness testimony of every stage. This mission introduces the questions; later missions will study named uprisings, participation and significance more closely. No points are awarded for harm, and no fighting or punishment is reenacted.

title: Prepare Your Causes and Forms Report
definition: What followed an action or process, as supported by evidence.
content: Review five ideas. A grievance is a reported concern, not every persons complete motive. Economic rules could affect work and choices in particular settings. Petitions and uprisings were different forms of action. Leaders, participants and affected residents were not automatically the same people. Causes, aims, actions and outcomes need their own supporting evidence. Prepare a fictional report for another Grade 5 learner. Name the case, place and period. Identify a concern, the recorded action and a supporting clue. Explain what remains uncertain. Do not label every request an independence uprising, assign motives from religion or ancestry, or treat a later painting as every participants testimony. Keep harm visible without reenacting it or earning points for it. The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. Review linked learning content before practice and a retry if needed. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.

reason: Explain particular concerns and forms of action through dated evidence while distinguishing participation, aims and outcomes.
